title: flaky-gpu-scheduler-rotation-run-notes-2026-12-08
content:
Purpose: quick notes from the on-call rotation where we ran a targeted scheduler rotation experiment to surface a recurring GPU node instability pattern. This is a working diary + rough runbook draft. Treat as ephemeral; we'll extract checklist bits into the formal runbook after the experiment is validated.

Summary of the incident window (2026-12-07 23:40 -> 2026-12-08 03:10 UTC):
- Symptoms: intermittent pod preemption + GPU device disappearances on nodes in rack r12 (zone eu-west-1a). Several pods reported CUDA context loss, then driver crash (nvidia), then kernel OOPS on two nodes. ECC correctable error counters spiked prior to driver resets on one node; on another node NVLink negotiation timeout observed.
- Visible impact: 14 active inference pods experienced 5-20s tail latency spikes; 3 pods evicted and restarted, causing transient request failures for customers on Dedicated clusters (customer-facing incident flagged).
- Initial hypothesis: thermal + power spike causing ECC bursts on older A100 nodes, compounded by NVLink retrain causing driver panic under high multi-process load.

What we ran during rotation (experiment plan):
1) Isolate a subset of suspected nodes (n-gpu-0123, n-gpu-0127, n-gpu-0131) and cordon them from new scheduling.
2) Reproduce load pattern: synthetic inference workload at 80% token throughput using the reproducible harness (linked in artifacts).
3) Toggle scheduler policy: switch from default balanced to soft-affinity packing (to reduce cross-node NVLink traffic) for 90 minutes.
4) Enable aggressive ECC scrubbing on node n-gpu-0127, monitor for clearable vs persistent correctable error counts.
5) Collect low-level traces: dmesg, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log, nv-hostengine logs, nvlink debug counters, and sysfs ECC counters every 30s.

Observations & raw notes (chronological):
- 23:50 UTC: after starting workload, n-gpu-0127 reported a steady ECC correctable increase (soft errors ~3/min). CPU temperatures rose ~6C but not outside normal.
- 00:05 UTC: driver reload triggered on n-gpu-0127 (nvidia persistence daemon restarted). No full kernel panic yet.
- 00:18 UTC: n-gpu-0131 NVLink retrain event (link 1->2), kernel printed nvlink negotiation timeout. Small number of dropped NVLink packets observed in counters.
- 00:25 UTC: under packed scheduling (co-located processes), memory bus contention appears higher; we measured 12% higher L2 cache misses vs balanced scheduling.
- 00:42 UTC: n-gpu-0123 produced a kernel oops with stack trace pointing to nvidia_uvm (user-space memory manager) and subsequent watchdog-triggered GPU reset.
- 01:10 UTC: ECC scrubbing on 0127 reduced correctable spike rate, but later errors still accumulate under sustained peak.
- 02:40 UTC: rotation revert to balanced scheduling; error rates fell to baseline.

Interpreting evidence (tentative conclusions):
- Two interacting problems: (A) hardware-correctable ECC bursts (likely memory channel-level glitches) that increase under thermal/power stress; (B) NVLink retrain timeouts when multiple heavy processes are co-located across links, which sometimes triggers driver path that assumes link stability and then escalates to kernel oops under race conditions.
- Packing pods increased local link utilization and memory pressure, amplifying both (A) and (B).
- ECC scrubbing helps but is not a panacea — persistent bursts indicate either failing DIMMs on the GPU board or a PCB trace/transceiver intermittency.

Actionable short-term mitigations (ops playbook draft):
- Immediate: when ECC correctable error rate per-GPU > 100/hour AND driver reload within 30 minutes -> auto-evacuate workload to warm spare pool and mark node for hardware review. Add threshold alert in Prometheus (gpu_ecc_correctable_total rate).
- Scheduling policy: introduce a per-cluster soft anti-affinity rule for process-heavy inference models where NVLink links are saturated. Default to balanced across NVLink islands for Dedicated clusters.
- Automated throttles: implement a token-bucket for bursty inference requests to reduce sustained 90%+ throughput durations that correlate with failures.
- Observability: surface nvlink_retrain_count_total and nvidia_driver_reload_total on service-level dashboards and per-route runbook pages. Add a small panel showing ECC correctable rate heatmap across racks.

Runbook draft (quick checklist for on-call):
- If an individual node reports ECC_correctable_rate > 50/min: (1) cordon the node, (2) drain non-critical workloads with grace period 120s, (3) run nvidia-smi -q -d ECC and capture /sys/class/infiniband for link state, (4) copy dmesg and nv-hostengine logs to /tmp and upload to gs://redwood-logs for triage.
- If NVLink retrain events > 3 in 30m on same node: (1) adjust scheduler to avoid cross-GPU packing for that node's pool, (2) check cabling and link topologies (if in colocation cage), (3) escalate to hardware team for link diagnostic run.
- If kernel oops with nvidia_uvm in stack: immediate isolation, collect vmcore (kexec/mahimahi) or the configured crashdump, and open high-priority hardware ticket.

Runbook automation ideas (follow-ups):
- Lambda to perform soft-evacuation when combined condition occurs: ECC_rate threshold AND driver_reload_count > 0 within window.
- Scheduler plugin that labels nodes as "nvlink-hot" when retrain rate high and prevents co-scheduling of heavy inference pods by default.
- Small agent on nodes to run self-test on GPU memory channels during low-util windows and report suspected DIMM/transceiver failures.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is there a correlation between specific firmware versions of the NVLink controller and the retrain timeouts? Need to compare firmware across affected nodes.
- Are DIMM-like failures on GPU boards more common in racks with older PDUs or with specific power distribution units? Cross-reference with dc-power telemetry.
- Can driver stack be hardened to avoid escalation from retrain timeout to kernel oops? Possibly a race in the uvm code. Need a PR from driver team.

Artifacts to keep and next experiments:
- Kept: the captured dmesg snippets, nvlink counters, ECC time-series, scheduler packing delta graphs (upload locations in linked_artifacts).
- Next experiment: swap a suspect GPU board into a known-good chassis and run prolonged ECC stress test (48h) to confirm hardware vs environmental cause.
- Also: test newer nvidia driver branch with additional NVLink retry/backoff logic in a staging pool for 72 hours.

Notes to self (informal):
- When summarizing for ops-runbook, separate immediate alarm thresholds from long-term flaky heuristics — on-call needs crisp actionables.
- Keep runbook steps idempotent and time-boxed; avoid lengthy manual shell surgery in the middle of traffic.
- Remember to tag customer-facing incident ticket with node IDs and time windows.

Appendix (useful commands & sample snippets):
- dmesg | grep -i nvlink  (sample: "nvlink: negotiation timeout on link 1:2")
- watch -n 1 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=ecc.errors.corrected.total --format=csv,noheader,nounits'
- cat /proc/driver/nvidia/params  (some systems expose debug knobs - document any changes before making them)
- kubectl cordon n-gpu-0127 && kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 n-gpu-0127

If you want to reuse this doc for the formal postmortem: we should expand the timeline with exact timestamps for each stack trace and paste the smallest reproducible kernel oops stack. For now: save this as working notes and extract two immediate tasks: (1) alerting threshold change, (2) schedule firmware audit for affected nodes.

Signed: Maya (on-call lead, rotation 2026-12-08)

Unresolved: I want to run a follow-up that toggles only the NVLink topology exposures (artificially pin processes to NVLink islands) to see if packing or thermal/power is dominant. Put on backlog and assign to Noah.
